lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.unitTitle: Body Signals, Rest, and Fueling Meals
lessonRef.title: Mastery check: sleep and recovery routines

standardsRefs: Ready for Life v1, Grade 4 Unit 4: Body Signals, Rest, and Fueling Meals
objective: Learners build a three-step wind-down routine for one night by pairing a specific space-clearing step with two new rest-signal steps, follow the routine, then the next morning compare how rested they feel to a typical morning and explain which specific step likely made the biggest difference.
scenario: A basic tidy routine only clears a space; a wind-down routine also helps a body get ready to rest. Building on a simple space-clearing habit, the learner adds two new pieces the night before: noticing a body signal that means rest time is getting close, and setting a consistent time to start winding down. The next morning, with a trusted adult, they check how the routine went.
safetyNotes: Share your three-step wind-down plan with a trusted adult before the first night so the adult knows what to expect.
If your routine includes dimming lights, adjusting a thermostat, or unplugging a device, check with a trusted adult first rather than changing household settings on your own.
This routine is about rest signals and steps only, never about how many hours you 'should' sleep or comparing your rest to anyone else's.

simulationAlternative.description: If the learner cannot complete an overnight routine before this lesson is reviewed, they instead plan the same three-step wind-down routine in writing (a specific space-clearing step, a named rest signal, and a set start time) and describe, based on a typical recent night, which step would most likely have made the biggest difference, explaining their reasoning the way they would after actually testing it.

materials: paper or a notes app for the routine plan
a way to check the time

tasks.directions: Before building your routine, think about a typical recent night.

prompts.text: Describe what usually happens in the thirty minutes before you try to fall asleep on a typical night.

tasks.directions: Build a three-step wind-down routine for tonight: first, clear and prepare your sleep space the way you'd clear any space for a task; second, notice and name one body signal that tells you rest time is getting close, like heavy eyelids or a slower mind; third, pick a consistent time to start the first two steps.

prompts.text: I wrote a specific space-clearing step for my sleep space, not just 'clean up.'
I named a specific body signal I'll watch for that means rest time is close.
I picked one consistent start time for tonight's routine.

tasks.directions: Follow your three-step routine tonight, then the next morning, with your trusted adult, compare how rested you feel to a typical morning and think back over which of the three steps mattered most.

prompts.text: Compared to a typical morning, how rested do you feel this morning?
Which of your three routine steps, space-clearing, noticing the rest signal, or the consistent start time, do you think made the biggest difference, and why?

tasks.directions: Think about how this routine compares to the simple space-clearing habit alone, without the rest-signal or timing steps.

prompts.text: Explain what the rest-signal and consistent-timing steps added beyond just clearing your space, and whether you will keep using the full three-step routine.

remediation: If a learner's routine stays at the space-clearing step alone and skips naming a specific rest signal, reteach by listing four example rest signals (heavy eyelids, yawning, slower thinking, restlessness) and having the learner circle the one that matches their own experience before finishing the routine plan.
extension: Have the learner test a second wind-down routine on a different night with the start time moved fifteen minutes earlier, and compare which of the two start times led to feeling more rested the next morning.
